items.title: How to debate, from a two-time world champion
items.description:
Two-time debate champion Bo Seo breaks down why arguments fail: the four bad-faith personas that hijack conversations, a four-question framework for picking fights worth having, and the surprising Cold War standoff between Nixon and Khrushchev that gives us a model for staying cool under pressure.  
 
 This video  How to debate, from a two-time world champion  is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: The gap between knowing better and doing better, and how to close it
items.description:
Most of us can recite the benefits of exercise, gratitude, and patience while doing none of it. Tal Ben-Shahar calls this the Knowing-Doing gap, and our typical interventions, like retreats and month-long overhauls, keep it open. 
 
 This video  The gap between knowing better and doing better, and how to close it  is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: Misery is an emotional feature, not a glitch in the system
items.description: Tolstoy’s famous opening to  Anna Karenina  (1878) about happy families being all alike but unhappy ones each being unhappy in their own way applies just as well to feelings. There are simply more ways to feel bad than to feel good — and more words to describe those bad feelings. English is bloated with terms for anger, anxiety, sorrow, shame, jealousy, regret. items.title: Ask Ethan: How did atoms come to be?
items.description: At the core of everything we’ve ever touched, seen, or interacted with here on Earth is the same humble physical structure: the atom. items.title: The information paradox at the heart of every black hole
items.description: When something falls into a black hole, where does the material ultimately go, and will it, or the quantum information that it contained, ever come back out again? According to Einstein’s general relativity, those answers are simple: as soon as anything physical — matter, antimatter, radiation, etc. — crosses over the event horizon, it’s irretrievably gone. items.title: Joanna Stern spent a year testing the AI future. Here’s what she learned.
items.description:
In the introduction to her new book,  I Am Not a Robot: My Year Using AI to Do (Almost) Everything , Joanna Stern describes a typical day in what could conceivably be all of our futures. Autonomous robots mow your lawn, fold your laundry, and drive you to your favorite restaurant.
